task: SW1 Fa0/1 is already a static access port. Enable its source-MAC security feature.

teaching.hint: Ordinary MAC learning alone does not impose a secure-address limit.
teaching.takeaway: Enabling port security establishes a limit and violation policy. It does not prove the identity of the device using an allowed MAC address.

task: Port security is enabled on Fa0/1. The approved phone-and-PC design needs exactly two secure MAC entries. Set that maximum.

teaching.hint: Count required secure entries, not just physical sockets.
teaching.takeaway: The maximum is the total allowed secure entries, not the number of additional devices. Check the phone/data VLAN behavior rather than assuming every phone always needs the same allowance.

task: On Fa0/1, port security is enabled and only the approved endpoint is connected. Make newly learned secure MAC addresses become configuration entries.

teaching.hint: Choose the learning method that records addresses in running configuration.
teaching.takeaway: Sticky learning records the learned addresses in running-config. Save afterward to retain them in startup-config; learning the first sender does not authenticate it.

task: Fa0/1 already has an approved secure-address list. Select the violation response that drops and reports unauthorized sources while continuing to forward permitted traffic.

teaching.hint: Compare reporting behavior and the effect on the entire port.
teaching.takeaway: Restrict drops violating traffic and records violations while permitted sources continue. Protect omits that reporting; shutdown disables the port.

task: A PC on Fa0/1 stopped communicating after an endpoint change. Inspect that port's security state, configured limit and violation count.

teaching.hint: Use the security-specific interface display, not only ordinary link status.
teaching.takeaway: Secure-shutdown identifies a current port-security outage. A nonzero historical violation count alone does not; compare current state and retest the approved endpoint after recovery.

task: DHCP snooping is disabled globally on SW1. Enable the feature; VLAN selection and trust will be configured separately.

teaching.hint: Enable the switch-wide feature before selecting client VLANs.
teaching.takeaway: Global enablement alone does not inspect every VLAN. Verify the intended VLAN list and the authorized server-reply ingress before testing a new client lease.

task: DHCP snooping is globally enabled on SW1, but VLAN 10 is not inspected. Enable inspection for that client VLAN.

teaching.hint: The global process and the list of inspected VLANs are separate settings.
teaching.takeaway: Both global enablement and VLAN selection are needed. A configured server-trust port cannot compensate for a client VLAN missing from the snooping policy.

task: You are configuring SW1 Gi0/1, where replies from the only authorized DHCP server enter. Permit those server replies through the snooping boundary; client ports remain untrusted.

teaching.hint: Follow the direction in which legitimate server messages enter this switch.
teaching.takeaway: Trust belongs on the verified server-reply ingress. A trunk is not automatically trustworthy, and client ports should not gain permission to send server replies.

task: A client obtained a lease after snooping was enabled. Display the switch records that associate its IP and MAC with a VLAN and access port.

teaching.hint: The switch learns these records from DHCP exchanges; the server keeps a different lease table.
teaching.takeaway: Compare the client's actual IP, MAC, VLAN and ingress port. A static printer may have no dynamic binding, and an old lease does not prove the switch observed a fresh exchange.

task: You are configuring SW1 Gi0/1, the controlled connection to a statically addressed router. The approved DAI design bypasses inspection only on this interface. Apply that trust.

teaching.hint: DHCP-message trust does not automatically permit ARP claims.
teaching.takeaway: DAI trust bypasses ARP inspection on this ingress. Keep endpoint ports inspected; the separate DHCP snooping trust setting does not provide this bypass.

task: Fresh snooping bindings and the controlled router-facing ARP policy are ready. Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on VLAN 10.

teaching.hint: ARP validation is a separate feature from DHCP-message inspection.
teaching.takeaway: DAI validates untrusted ARP claims against permitted bindings or policy. Prepare legitimate static-host exceptions before enabling it; an address exclusion alone does not authorize ARP.

task: On SW1 Fa0/2, configure broadcast suppression at 1% utilization and recovery below 0.5%, using percentage thresholds on a supporting Catalyst.

teaching.hint: The first threshold enters suppression; the second controls when it ends.
teaching.takeaway: The falling threshold must not exceed the rising threshold. These percentages measure the configured traffic class; storm suppression does not repair the underlying loop or traffic source.

task: On a supporting Catalyst, policy HOSTS incorrectly has the router role. You are inside that policy. Correct its role for ordinary endpoint ports that must reject router advertisements.

teaching.hint: An ordinary endpoint is not an authorized IPv6 router.
teaching.takeaway: The host role rejects router messages under this policy. The policy must still be attached to the correct endpoint ports; defining it alone changes no ingress behavior.

task: On a supporting Catalyst, you are configuring endpoint port Gi1/0/1. Policy HOSTS already has the host role. Attach it here so endpoint-originated router advertisements are filtered.

teaching.hint: A policy definition has no effect on a port until it is applied there.
teaching.takeaway: Attach the host-role policy at the endpoint ingress. An authorized router needs its own permitted boundary; a policy name alone does not establish either role or enforcement.
